title: ProRB: a structure-free unified framework for joint prediction and design of protein-RNA interactions.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed Q-BioLiP's protein-RNA annotation table (PRNA_nonredund_annotation.csv, 4.4 MB, 5,077 rows, 2,638 structure assemblies, 0 missing labels) and its matching protein sequence archive (2,638 FASTA files, 34,522 chain sequences); counted 951,024 RNA-contacting residue annotations over 6,243,961 residues in 30,365 labelled chains (15.2% positive), 11,777 unique protein sequences. Tested whether the residue numbers in the label column line up with the supplied sequences: they do not out of the box (only ~30% of residues match), but one integer offset per chain fixes 4,668 of 5,631 sampled chain segments exactly (83.4% match at least 95% of residues). Also downloaded the main Q-BioLiP non-redundant annotation (42.7 MB, 179,354 rows; 3,065 pure-RNA ligand rows, UniProt accession present for 3,231 of 3,434 RNA rows) and the CoPRA mCSM_RNA archive (18.6 MB: 214 cross-validation rows + 79 blind-test rows of experimental binding free energy change, with protein, mutant and RNA sequences in the table). Extracted the paper's supplementary Word file and read all its results tables.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The 201-pair affinity benchmark (PRA201) and the 30,006-pair pretraining set (PRI30K): the 91 MB PRA310.zip download timed out twice and PRI30k.zip is 2.56 GB, over the size cap, so their contents are unverified. The paper's own processed binding-site dataset and its cluster splits (821-1,448 protein clusters at 40-90% identity) are not released anywhere I could find. The Zenodo code record (10.5281/zenodo.21447682) could not be reached from this environment (repeated TLS handshake timeouts), so ProRB's code and weights are taken from the paper's statement only.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: Q-BioLiP annotation CSV and sequence archive download with no login; CoPRA data is public on HuggingFace under an MIT licence. Only the paper's own Zenodo code record was unreachable here.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the protein side the label is a column: Binding_residue lists every residue contacting the RNA, 0 missing in 5,077 rows. It needs a per-chain numbering offset to sit on the sequence (verified fixable for 83%). The RNA (nucleotide) side is NOT in the table and would have to be built from 736 MB of ligand structures.

a3_inputs_present.note: Protein sequences are in the downloaded FASTA archive (34,522 chains, all labelled chains covered). The partner RNA sequence is absent (only 8 of 34,522 chains are RNA) and would need one bulk sequence download from the structure database, not per-item lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Label is binary contact, defined by a heavy-atom distance cutoff in the Q-BioLiP documentation; the affinity tables use kcal/mol explicitly (paper text and the mCSM_RNA table's DDG column).

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified in files: 11,777 unique labelled protein sequences, 30,365 labelled chains, 951,024 positive residues. Note the paper's own affinity set is only 201 pairs and its mutation set only 293 rows - both far too small on their own.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3 GB (4.4 MB labels + 3.7 MB sequences + cached per-residue embeddings for 11,777 unique sequences)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Small protein language model checkpoints on CPU; embeddings streamed to disk in chunks keeps memory well under 16 GB.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Downloads are internally consistent (5,077 annotation rows, 2,638 assemblies, all with sequences). The paper gives no raw complex count for its binding-site set, only cluster counts, and its processed split is unreleased, so exact reproduction of its numbers is impossible - a caveat, not a contradiction.

a8_label_provenance.note: Contacts come from experimentally solved complexes by a distance rule, not from any model, and are not computable from the sequence features. The mCSM_RNA table does carry two other models' predictions as separate columns, which must be dropped as features.

B1.why: Two sources: one label CSV plus 2,638 FASTA files; join on assembly plus chain works after a numbering fix.

B2.why: Label CSV and FASTA archive both parsed first try with pandas; no encoding or delimiter problems.

B3.why: All contact labels come from one pipeline (distance cutoff on solved structures), so they are directly comparable.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values; Binding_residue is non-missing in all 5,077 rows I read.

B5.why: 30,365 labelled chains collapse to 11,777 unique sequences; large assemblies (ribosomes) repeat chains, so dedup is needed.

B6.why: Main annotation has a readme, but the residue-numbering convention is undocumented and demonstrably mismatched to the supplied sequences.

C1.why: Partner-RNA ablation is informative either way, but any headline claim means beating GPSite's published 0.573 area under precision-recall.

C2.why: Several open, honestly split models on this exact task: GPSite, GraphBind, EquiPNAS, ESM-NBR, MPBind, CLAPE; searched and retrieved.

C3.why: Partner-specific interface prediction was critically assessed in 2019 and is pursued again by ProRB and CORAL in 2026.

C4.why: Alternative is solving a complex structure or scanning mutations in the lab - slow and expensive.

C5.why: Published numbers exist (GPSite 0.573, GraphBind 0.506, ProRB 0.12-0.17 protein side) plus a 15.2% positive-rate dummy I computed.

D1.why: ESM-2 protein language model and RNA-FM RNA language model both have open downloadable weights.

D2.why: Per-residue embeddings for 11,777 unique sequences cache once on CPU; only a small classifier head trains.

D3.why: ESM-2 and RNA-FM are MIT-licensed; CoPRA data card states MIT; Q-BioLiP terms unstated but downloads are open.

E1.why: Sequence-identity clustering of the 11,777 unique sequences, plus a deposition-year split using the PDB IDs in the table.

E2.why: Thousands of identity clusters expected from 11,777 unique sequences; far more than the five needed.

E3.why: Dummy baselines computable: 15.2% positive rate overall, plus a per-amino-acid propensity baseline.

E4.why: Same sequence appears in many assemblies (30,365 chains, 11,777 sequences), so label disagreement across complexes gives a ceiling.

E5.why: Positive controls available: arginine/lysine enrichment at interfaces, and recovery of known RNA-recognition-motif domain interfaces.

E6.why: Label shuffling within chain and feature-block ablation (protein only versus protein plus RNA) are both trivial here.

E7.why: GraphBind and GPSite publish their own test sets, and PDB deposition dates allow a genuine temporal split.

E8.why: GPSite's code is open so its number is reproducible; ProRB's own number is not, because its split is unreleased.

G1.why: UniProt accessions in 3,231 of 3,434 RNA rows and PDB identifiers everywhere - verified in the main annotation file.

G2.why: AlphaFold structure database and InterPro domain families both join on the UniProt accession already present.

G3.why: One assembly maps to many chains and one protein to many structures; workable with a collapse rule, not one-to-one.

G4.why: Combination mostly re-asks what GPSite already answers with predicted structures, so the gain is marginal.

H1.why: Non-contacting residues are systematically recorded inside every solved complex: 84.8% of residues are negatives.

H2.why: Protein Data Bank-wide so many species, but dominated by crystallisable complexes and large ribosomal assemblies.

H3.why: Honest claim is writable in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3 field).

H4.why: Q-BioLiP documents its construction, but the paper does not discuss the bias toward crystallisable complexes.

I1.why: Users are method developers (the GPSite and ProRB groups) plus structural RNA-binding-protein labs - a community more than a named customer.

I2.why: A negative partner-RNA result would redirect method design, but would not change any bench experiment.

I3.why: Area under precision-recall and precision in the top-k residues match the real decision: which residues to mutate.

I4.why: Simple amino-acid propensity already gets part of the way; language models help but the task is partly a lookup.

J1.why: Real transfer learning, grouped splits and honest evaluation - exactly the ML skills targeted.

J2.why: Sanity checks are obvious to a biologist: basic residues at interfaces, known RNA-binding domains.

J3.why: A cleanly numbered per-residue protein-RNA interface table would be shareable even if the model is mediocre.

J4.why: No time budget written; realistically three to four weeks including benchmark rebuilding.

J5.why: No kill date recorded; informal condition would be the partner-RNA ablation showing no effect.

existing_models.name: ProRB (this paper, 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Protein-side interface area under precision-recall 0.122-0.171 and RNA-side 0.208-0.266, on sequence-identity cluster splits at 40-90% identity; binding free energy correlation 0.46-0.53 on 201 pairs. Its own supplement shows a plain one-hot encoding beating it on the protein side at two thresholds (0.129 versus 0.122; 0.138 versus 0.131).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation to complexes unlike the training data, and the lack of any wet-lab test of its designed RNA sequences.

existing_models.name: GPSite (eLife 2024, github.com/biomed-AI/GPSite)
existing_models.score_and_split: RNA-binding residue area under precision-recall 0.573 on its published held-out test set, sequence-identity filtered; beats structure-based methods.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Reliance on predicted structures for hard targets; no partner-specific prediction.

existing_models.name: GraphBind
existing_models.score_and_split: RNA-binding residue area under precision-recall 0.506 with experimental structures, dropping to 0.433 with predicted structures (as reported by GPSite's benchmark).

existing_models.name: EquiPNAS (Nucleic Acids Research 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Protein-nucleic acid binding residue prediction using protein-language-model-informed equivariant graph networks, evaluated on sequence-identity-filtered benchmarks derived from BioLiP/Q-BioLiP.

existing_models.name: CoPRA (AAAI 2025, github.com/hanrthu/CoPRA)
existing_models.score_and_split: Binding free energy prediction on the 310-pair PRA310 set; Pearson correlation 0.287-0.370 on the splits used in this paper's supplement.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Tiny labelled affinity data (hundreds of pairs).

existing_models.name: Partner-specific RNA-binding residue assessment (Proteins 2019)
existing_models.score_and_split: A critical assessment finding that partner-specific predictors are outperformed by partner-agnostic state of the art when judged on partner-agnostic metrics.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Whether partner information can ever be exploited usefully at residue level.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model) plus RNA-FM (RNA language model)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU; small ESM-2 checkpoint, embeddings cached once

integration.partner_dataset: AlphaFold structure database and InterPro domain families
integration.join_key: UniProt accession (present for 3,231 of 3,434 RNA-ligand rows I checked)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do RNA-contacting residues cluster on predicted structural surfaces and within specific domain families in ways a sequence-only model misses - a question GPSite already largely answers with predicted structures.

controls.positive_control: Interfaces must come out enriched in arginine and lysine, and the model must rank known RNA-recognition-motif and K-homology domain surfaces highest.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle contact labels within each chain and confirm performance collapses to the 15.2% positive-rate baseline; ablate the RNA input block.
controls.external_validation: GPSite's and GraphBind's published RNA-binding test sets, plus a split on Protein Data Bank deposition year.

honest_claim_h3: Among protein chains that have been crystallised in complex with RNA, a frozen protein-language-model head predicts which residues touch the RNA at a stated precision-recall score on held-out sequence-identity clusters, and adding the partner RNA sequence changes that score by a stated amount.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein sequence, with or without its partner RNA sequence, to predict which residues touch the RNA.
plain_idea.train_on: Protein chains from solved protein-RNA complexes, each residue labelled as touching the RNA or not: 11,777 unique protein sequences, 30,365 labelled chains, 6,243,961 residues, which I counted in the downloaded files.
plain_idea.predict: A binary flag per residue. The truth comes from the experimentally solved three-dimensional structure, where a residue counts as contacting if its nearest heavy atom is within a fixed distance of the RNA.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Method developers want to know whether knowing the actual RNA partner improves interface prediction at all, or whether models are just learning generic sticky surfaces; a clear answer either way guides how these tools are built.

more_or_better_data.why: The large labelled set is Q-BioLiP, the same resource GPSite, GraphBind and EquiPNAS already train on; this paper's own data adds only 201 affinity pairs and 293 mutation measurements.

confidence_score.why: The same protein appears in many complexes (30,365 chains from 11,777 unique sequences), so label disagreement across complexes could give per-residue uncertainty, which none of the named models report.

models_beatable.why: GPSite (2024, protein language model plus geometric network, 0.573 area under precision-recall on an identity-filtered test set) and EquiPNAS (2024) are recent, open and honestly evaluated; a frozen-embedding head on a laptop is unlikely to beat them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Adding the partner RNA sequence is not guaranteed to help - the 2019 critical assessment found partner-specific methods lose to partner-agnostic ones - and the RNA sequences are not even in the downloaded files, so the input differs from the baselines' input.

ml_idea: Rebuild a per-residue protein-RNA interface benchmark from Q-BioLiP (verified: 5,077 annotated sites, 11,777 unique protein sequences, 951,024 contacting residues, 15.2% positive) and test whether conditioning on the partner RNA sequence improves residue-level prediction over a protein-only frozen ESM-2 head, evaluated on sequence-identity clusters and a deposition-year split.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: 11,777 unique sequences of median length 138 (counted in the files) through a small ESM-2 checkpoint on CPU, embeddings written to disk in chunks; the head is a small classifier over roughly 2.4 million deduplicated residues.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Cluster the 11,777 unique protein sequences at 30% identity and check how many clusters are absent from GPSite's and GraphBind's training sets - if almost none are, there is no new data here and the project is only a re-evaluation.

verdict_reason: The paper's own labelled data is far too small to model (201 binding-affinity pairs, 293 mutation measurements), and the one large labelled target behind it - RNA-contacting residues from Q-BioLiP, which I downloaded and verified at 951,024 positives over 11,777 unique sequences - is the most saturated task in this subfield, with GPSite (0.573 area under precision-recall, open code), GraphBind, EquiPNAS, ESM-NBR and MPBind all openly published on identity-filtered splits. The interesting twist, whether the partner RNA sequence helps at residue level, was critically assessed in 2019 with a negative answer and is being pursued again by ProRB and CORAL; worse, the partner RNA sequences and the nucleotide-side labels are not in the downloadable files at all. Worth recording for someone else: this paper's own supplement shows a plain one-hot baseline beating its full model on the protein side at two identity thresholds, and its processed splits are unreleased, so even a re-evaluation cannot be made exact.
